name: The Adlestrop churchyard yew

location.address: St Mary Magdalene churchyard, Adlestrop, Gloucestershire GL56 0YN

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, tree 3969 (Ancient 5-7 m)

access: Open churchyard (Ancient Yew Group lists access as public; church parochial church council ground). Free, no opening hours.
transport: Adlestrop village near Moreton-in-Marsh (nearest mainline station, roughly 6 km); car or taxi.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the two ivy-covered trunks joined near the ground, with a curved seat round the south side. It stands by the west wall of the churchyard, west of the tower, beside a stone lean-to shed.
verify_notes: AYG: ancient yew unrecorded until Lin Carter found it in 2012; Tim Hills recorded a male yew of two trunks joined near the ground, girth 20 ft 9 in (633 cm at 5 cm; 2012, Hills; repeated 2017 Norton), larger fragment 14 ft 1 in, smaller 10 ft 4 in, ivy-covered. Hills judges the two trunks look like sections of a once larger tree. AYG classifies girth 5-7 m as ancient, likely age above 500 years (AYG's own banding: derived age, broad). Site file dated 2024 and girth grid 2017 give recent revisits (alive). Church: tower 14th/15th century, rest 1750-1764. Source: AYG only (specialist register, three separate recorders), flagged 'one source'. Ground held by the Parochial Church Council; open churchyard. Position AYG grid SP24302690 converted; approximate. Girth is the whole-tree girth near the ground at 5 cm, so it overstates a normal 1.5 m girth: state as 'near the ground'. Ancient Yew Group girth grid for Gloucestershire: https://ancient-yew.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Gloucestershire-girth-grid-v2.pdf
story:
Until 2012 nobody had written this yew down. It had stood by the west wall of this Cotswold churchyard for centuries, and the Ancient Yew Group only added it to their register after Lin Carter found it that year. Then Tim Hills came to measure, and the tape went round to 6.33 metres, taken near the ground where the two trunks meet.

Two trunks, because this is a split tree. It is a male yew in two fragments joined low down, the larger about 14 feet round and the smaller about 10, both heavily wrapped in ivy. Hills thought they looked like sections of one once larger tree. The girth is measured around both together at the base, so it reads bigger than a chest-height figure would.

The Ancient Yew Group's girth bands put a yew of this size in the ancient class, likely over 500 years. That is an estimate from size, not a dating, but on it the yew is older than most of St Mary Magdalene's church, whose tower is 14th or 15th century and whose body was rebuilt between 1750 and 1764.

Someone has put a curved seat round its south side. It is the right instinct. This is a tree for sitting next to, slowly.

name: The Coln Rogers churchyard yew

location.address: St Andrew's Church, Coln Rogers, Gloucestershire GL54 3JZ

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, tree 367 (Ancient 5-7 m)

access: Open churchyard (Ancient Yew Group lists access as public; church parochial church council ground). Free, no opening hours.
transport: Coln Rogers, a village in the Coln valley north-east of Cirencester; no railway; car or taxi.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the large yew south-west of St Andrew's, the small Grade I church with Saxon walls. It stands in the churchyard on that side of the building.
verify_notes: AYG (Tim Hills, visited 18 Sep 1999): yew grows to the SW of the church; 574 cm at 30 cm; girth grid: 18 ft 6 in to 19 ft 10 in over 1999 Hills, with 18 ft 10 in in 2013 Norton (two recorders; stable). Site file dated 2019 (alive). Parts of the church are Saxon (AYG); Wikipedia puts the Saxon church in the 11th century. Gloucestershire Places of Worship quotes Kelly's Directory 1923 describing 'a splendid old yew' (seen only in a search summary, not fetched; treat as unconfirmed). AYG band 5-7 m = ancient, likely above 500 years (derived). Source AYG only: flagged 'one source'. Position AYG grid SP08740968 converted; approximate. Ancient Yew Group girth grid for Gloucestershire: https://ancient-yew.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Gloucestershire-girth-grid-v2.pdf
story:
The church beside this yew still has walls the Saxons built. St Andrew's at Coln Rogers is a small Grade I church in the Coln valley, and parts of it are Saxon, from the 11th century by Wikipedia's dating. The yew grows to its south-west, in the small churchyard.

What is striking about the tree is how little its numbers move. Tim Hills put it at between 18 feet 6 and 19 feet 10 inches when he visited in September 1999. Peter Norton came back in 2013 and found 18 feet 10. The Ancient Yew Group's current figure is 574 centimetres at 30 centimetres off the ground. Fourteen years and two recorders, and the tree is essentially the size it was. Measuring an old yew tells you how big it is far better than how old.

That is why the age here is a band, not a date. The Group's girth classes place a yew between five and seven metres in the ancient category, likely over 500 years. Nobody has dated this one, and its exact age is a question we would like answered.

What you get on the day is the pairing, a quiet valley church with Saxon stonework and, beside it, a yew the Group counts as ancient.

name: The Hawling churchyard yew

location.address: St Edward's Church, Hawling, near Winchcombe, Gloucestershire GL54 5SZ

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, tree 1461 (Ancient 5-7 m)

access: Open churchyard (Ancient Yew Group lists access as public; church parochial church council ground). Free, no opening hours.
transport: Hawling, a hamlet near Winchcombe; no regular public transport found; car or taxi.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the hollow trunk with an opening on its north-west side, at the edge of a drop to the old dairy. It stands in the north-west corner of St Edward's churchyard; a younger yew grows to its north-east.
verify_notes: AYG: female yew, 549 cm at 30 cm (2003 Hills); girth grid 18 ft 0 in to 18 ft 6 in in 2014 (Hills/Norton, about 564 cm; girth_cm uses 18 ft 6 in = 564 cm at 3 ft); Allen Meredith 1988: approximately 18 ft. Three independent recorders over 26 years, stable. Hills' 2019 site file: hollow on the NW side, large hollow spaces, tree 'in vigorous good health' (2003); in 1936 Mee wrote of 'a gigantic yew' but Hills sees nothing suggesting recent gigantic size (so state girth, not 'gigantic'). Site file 2019 shows revisit (alive). AYG band 5-7 m = ancient, likely above 500 years (derived). Church Grade II* (Historic England 1091850): sections early 13th century, nave and chancel rebuilt 1764. Source AYG only with Historic England for the church: flagged. Position AYG grid SP06292294 converted, approximate. Geograph 90180 shows the church (not the yew). Ancient Yew Group girth grid for Gloucestershire: https://ancient-yew.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Gloucestershire-girth-grid-v2.pdf
story:
In 1936 Arthur Mee called this a gigantic yew. Its modern recorder sees nothing to suggest it has been gigantic in recent times, and the tape backs him. Allen Meredith put it at about 18 feet in 1988. Tim Hills found 549 centimetres in 2003, and by 2014 it was 18 feet 6, about 564 centimetres. Three recorders across 26 years, and the figure has hardly moved. So we report the girth and leave the adjectives to Mee.

It is a female yew, hollow, with large spaces inside and an opening on its north-west side. Hills recorded it in vigorous good health in 2003. The Ancient Yew Group's girth bands place it in the ancient class, likely over 500 years, an estimate from size rather than a dating.

The setting is half the visit. Hawling is a hamlet near Winchcombe, and the yew stands in the north-west corner of St Edward's churchyard, right on the edge of a vertical drop down to the old dairy. The church has 13th-century sections, with a nave and chancel rebuilt in 1764. A younger female yew grows to the north-east, a reminder that the older one was once that size too.

name: The Kemble churchyard yew

location.address: All Saints Church, Kemble, Gloucestershire GL7 6AD

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, tree 531 (Ancient 4-5 m)

access: Open churchyard (Ancient Yew Group lists access as public; church parochial church council ground). Free, no opening hours.
transport: Kemble village, close to Kemble railway station (about 1 km) (direct trains from London Paddington and Swindon).
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by how close it grows to the church, only about two metres from the wall of All Saints. It stands in the churchyard in the middle of the village, about a kilometre from Kemble station.
verify_notes: AYG (Tim Hills, 28 Sep 1998): yew grows only 2 m from the building; 490 cm at 110 cm (2011 Hills); girth grid: 18 ft 6 in at 6 ft (1894, Wiltshire arch.), 20 ft (1938 Mee), 15 ft 8 in (1998 Hills), 16 ft 1 in (2011 Hills), 16 ft 1 in at 3 ft 6 in (2015 Norton). Earlier figures (1894, 1938) are larger and measured at different heights; the modern ones are consistent at about 490 cm (girth_cm 490 = AYG 2011 figure at 110 cm). AYG site file and photos dated 2026 (alive). AYG band 4-5 m = ancient; derived age broad. Source AYG with the diocese-wide grid: flagged 'one source'. Position AYG grid ST98929698 converted; approximate. Ancient Yew Group girth grid for Gloucestershire: https://ancient-yew.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Gloucestershire-girth-grid-v2.pdf
story:
On paper this yew has been shrinking for a century. In 1894 a Wiltshire archaeological journal recorded 18 feet 6 inches. In 1938 Arthur Mee gave 20 feet. Tim Hills measured 15 feet 8 in 1998, and 16 feet 1 in 2011, which Peter Norton matched in 2015. The tree has not lost four feet. The early figures were taken at different heights on the trunk, and where you hold the tape on a yew changes everything. The modern readings agree at about 4.9 metres, and that is the number we use.

It grows just two metres from the wall of All Saints, nearer the building than you would think a tree of this size could stand. The Ancient Yew Group's girth bands class a yew of this size as ancient. On that basis the estimate is broad, several hundred years, somewhere between about 300 and 600, with no dating behind it.

You can reach it without a car. Kemble station, with direct trains from London Paddington and Swindon, is about a kilometre from the churchyard, and the yew is the tree pressed against the church.
